content.text:
**Prompt Interpretation:** You want me to research whether Keir Starmer “values human rights,” and to demonstrate that with verifiable, up‑to‑date evidence. You also want every source I use listed with a summary and a trust assessment so you can judge the evidence yourself.

**Reasoning Process:** I can’t provide my private, step‑by‑step chain‑of‑thought. Instead, here’s a concise description of my approach: 
- I identified concrete, checkable indicators of valuing human rights: (a) explicit treaty commitments (e.g., remaining in the ECHR), (b) government policy decisions with direct human‑rights implications (e.g., scrapping the Rwanda scheme; introducing a Hillsborough “duty of candour” law), (c) official statements supporting international humanitarian law and rights protections, and (d) Starmer’s professional record in human‑rights law. 
- I searched recent, reputable sources (official government pages, parliamentary records, BBC/Reuters/FT/Politico) and major NGOs (Amnesty, Human Rights Watch) for evidence after 1 July 2024 (he became PM on 5 July 2024) to ensure relevance.
- I cross‑checked multiple outlets for each point and included primary sources (GOV.UK, Hansard) wherever possible.

**Assumptions:** 
- “Values human rights” is interpreted as: makes binding commitments to human‑rights frameworks; takes decisions aligning government policy with human‑rights obligations; and has a consistent record (before and after taking office) that places weight on rights protections. 
- “Proof” in politics is evidentiary rather than mathematical—so I present converging evidence from high‑trust sources. 
- You prefer breadth (several strong, diverse sources) over quantity of weaker links.

**Final Answer:** 
Conclusion (one‑sentence summary): On the evidence, Keir Starmer has repeatedly and explicitly committed the UK to human‑rights norms (notably remaining in the ECHR), reversed a high‑profile policy widely criticised on human‑rights grounds (the Rwanda scheme), advanced accountability legislation (Hillsborough Law), and has a longstanding professional record in human‑rights law—together forming strong proof that he values human rights. 

Evidence set (each with URL, summary, trust, reasoning):

1) 
- URL: https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/articles/cz9dn8erg3zo 
- Summary: On 6 July 2024 (day one as PM), Starmer declared the Rwanda deportation scheme “dead and buried,” calling it ineffective and a gimmick; Labour would replace it with other measures. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: BBC News is a high‑reliability UK public broadcaster; the piece reports a first press conference and direct quotes. ([feeds.bbci.co.uk](https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/articles/cz9dn8erg3zo?utm_source=openai))

2) 
- URL: https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/new-uk-pm-starmer-confirms-end-rwanda-asylum-deportation-scheme-2024-07-06/ 
- Summary: Reuters corroborates the termination of the Rwanda plan, noting legal concerns and that critics saw it as immoral and impractical. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Reuters is a globally respected wire service; this independently confirms the BBC report. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/new-uk-pm-starmer-confirms-end-rwanda-asylum-deportation-scheme-2024-07-06/?utm_source=openai))

3) 
- URL: https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/articles/c05m6mvq45lo 
- Summary: On 4 March 2025, the UK confirmed no further payments to Rwanda after scrapping the deal; Rwanda had asked for remaining money, but the UK said no more will be paid. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: BBC provides official statements and updates on financial implications of ending the scheme. ([feeds.bbci.co.uk](https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/articles/c05m6mvq45lo?utm_source=openai))

4) 
- URL: https://www.amnesty.org.uk/press-releases/uk-scrapping-unlawful-rwanda-refugee-scheme-welcome 
- Summary: Amnesty International UK welcomed the scheme’s scrapping as restoring a rights‑respecting approach to asylum; urges fair processing and safe routes. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Amnesty is a leading human‑rights NGO; statement aligns with Supreme Court findings and international law critiques. ([amnesty.org.uk](https://www.amnesty.org.uk/press-releases/uk-scrapping-unlawful-rwanda-refugee-scheme-welcome?utm_source=openai))

5) 
- URL: https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/11/15/uk-supreme-court-finds-uk-rwanda-asylum-scheme-unlawful 
- Summary: Human Rights Watch explains the UK Supreme Court’s ruling that Rwanda was not a safe third country and removals risked refoulement—context for why ending the scheme aligns with rights obligations. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: HRW is a reputable NGO; although pre‑July 2024, it supplies the legal rights context underpinning the later decision to scrap the plan. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/11/15/uk-supreme-court-finds-uk-rwanda-asylum-scheme-unlawful?utm_source=openai))

6) 
- URL: https://www.politico.eu/article/britain-keir-starmer-never-leave-european-convention-human-rights-political-community-summit/ 
- Summary: In November 2024 Starmer vowed the UK would “never” leave the ECHR, linking that to a humane migration approach and scrapping Rwanda. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Politico is a high‑quality political outlet; quotes are consistent with other reporting. ([politico.eu](https://www.politico.eu/article/britain-keir-starmer-never-leave-european-convention-human-rights-political-community-summit/?utm_source=openai))

7) 
- URL: https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/keir-starmer-shabana-mahmood-government-prime-minister-liberal-democrat-b1245793.html 
- Summary: In September 2025, Starmer told MPs it would be a “profound mistake” to quit the ECHR; Justice Secretary Mahmood said leaving would align the UK with Russia/Belarus. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: The Standard reports direct Commons/Lords statements; independently confirms the government’s ECHR commitment. ([standard.co.uk](https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/keir-starmer-shabana-mahmood-government-prime-minister-liberal-democrat-b1245793.html?utm_source=openai))

8) 
- URL: https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/lords/2024-07-25/LordsChamber 
- Summary: Lords ministerial statement (25 July 2024): “the UK is unequivocally committed to the ECHR,” and promoting human rights as British values. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Hansard is the official parliamentary record—primary documentation of the government’s stance. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/lords/2024-07-25/LordsChamber?utm_source=openai))

9) 
- URL: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/echr-must-evolve-to-restore-public-confidence-in-rule-of-law-says-lord-chancellor 
- Summary: 18 June 2025: the Lord Chancellor affirmed the UK is “resolutely committed to the ECHR,” while advocating reforms to maintain public confidence. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Official GOV.UK press release; primary source for government policy. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/echr-must-evolve-to-restore-public-confidence-in-rule-of-law-says-lord-chancellor?utm_source=openai))

10) 
- URL: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/hillsborough-law-to-ensure-truth-never-concealed-by-state-again 
- Summary: 15 Sept 2025: Government introduced “Hillsborough Law”—a statutory duty of candour on public bodies, parity of legal representation for bereaved families—delivering a manifesto pledge on accountability and victims’ rights. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Official policy announcement; clear rights‑enhancing measures on state accountability. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/hillsborough-law-to-ensure-truth-never-concealed-by-state-again?utm_source=openai))

11) 
- URL: https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10359/ 
- Summary: House of Commons Library briefing on the Public Office (Accountability) Bill (“Hillsborough Law”): explains the duty of candour, new offences, and support for families at inquests. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Commons Library is non‑partisan, authoritative parliamentary analysis. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10359/?utm_source=openai))

12) 
- URL: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hillsborough-law-bill 
- Summary: Policy paper and bill documents (16 Sept 2025) detailing the duty of candour, parity of arms for families, and misconduct in public office reforms. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Primary legislation materials on GOV.UK. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hillsborough-law-bill?utm_source=openai))

13) 
- URL: https://www.ft.com/content/ccbbf678-7319-4c4d-831f-f6441b2fb1ed 
- Summary: FT profile recounts Starmer’s background as a leading human‑rights barrister (McLibel, Northern Ireland and African rights cases) and later as DPP. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: The Financial Times is a high‑reputation outlet; this supports the long‑standing professional human‑rights record. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/ccbbf678-7319-4c4d-831f-f6441b2fb1ed?utm_source=openai))

14) 
- URL: https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2025-05-06/CommonsChamber 
- Summary: PM’s 6 May 2025 statement condemns attacks on civilians, calls for immediate ceasefire, aid, and respect for humanitarian law in Gaza; announces UK humanitarian support and medical evacuations for children. 
- Trust: TRUSTED 
- Reasoning: Hansard is the official record; demonstrates commitment to humanitarian protections and international law. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2025-05-06/CommonsChamber?utm_source=openai))

How this evidence adds up:
- Policy alignment with human rights: Ending the Rwanda scheme removed a policy the Supreme Court and rights groups viewed as breaching non‑refoulement; rights NGOs welcomed the move. ([feeds.bbci.co.uk](https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/articles/cz9dn8erg3zo?utm_source=openai))
- Binding international commitments: Starmer’s government has repeatedly and publicly ruled out leaving the ECHR and affirmed commitment in Parliament and via official channels. ([politico.eu](https://www.politico.eu/article/britain-keir-starmer-never-leave-european-convention-human-rights-political-community-summit/?utm_source=openai))
- Strengthening domestic accountability: The Hillsborough Law advances victims’ and families’ rights and imposes candour duties on public bodies—core rule‑of‑law and human‑rights accountability measures. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/hillsborough-law-to-ensure-truth-never-concealed-by-state-again?utm_source=openai))
- Consistent record: Starmer’s legal career focused heavily on human‑rights cases, underscoring a longstanding orientation toward rights protections. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/ccbbf678-7319-4c4d-831f-f6441b2fb1ed?utm_source=openai))

Nuance: The government has also argued for recalibrating aspects of how rights are applied (e.g., refining Article 8 usage; advocating ECHR reforms) while explicitly maintaining UK membership and commitments—so the stance is “pro‑rights within the system,” not “leave the system.” ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/echr-must-evolve-to-restore-public-confidence-in-rule-of-law-says-lord-chancellor?utm_source=openai))

Overall conclusion: Across treaty commitments, policy choices, legislation, official statements, and professional background, there is strong, multi‑source evidence that Keir Starmer values human rights.
